source_note: Transcribed from High-School-Course-Catalog-26-27-1.pdf (24 pages) and verified against the source PDF; the earlier copy-paste that was truncated at 'Psychology and Sociology' has been fully reconciled. Three courses appear in the department index but carry NO description in the PDF's course-detail pages and are genuinely undescribed (description=null): 'Illustration and Graphic Design' (Business/Comms/Media), Agriculture 'Independent Study', and 'Technical Drawing' (Waubonsee Engineering). 'Dual Credit Chemistry' is also listed with credits/grade but no description. Repeated FFA/SAE boilerplate in Agriculture descriptions was condensed to '(FFA activities and SAE projects are an integral component.)'. Where the department index and detail pages disagree on a course's name or credit, the detail page is authoritative and the index value is preserved in an 'index_*' or note field.

grading_legend.honors_star: * Honors: 0.5 GPA escalator; faculty recommendation; weighted grades; placement reassessed each year; assumes no in-class remediation of basic skills
grading_legend.dual_credit_star2: ** Dual credit: earns both high school and college credit; 1.0 GPA escalator
grading_legend.ap_star3: *** AP: must take the AP exam in May for possible college exemption; 1.0 GPA escalator

mission: Develop graduates characterized as scholars, disciple makers, and influencers.

scholars: Scholarly knowledge of the Bible as God's inspired Word, the foundation of all truth and life
Understand and embrace the essential doctrines of the Christian faith
Comprehensive command of communication fundamentals (speaking, listening, writing, reading)
Proficient in mathematics and science, can use the scientific method, and see God's created order
Appreciation and skills within literature and how it expresses and shapes beliefs and values
Effectively and ethically use technology to communicate and to find, analyze, and evaluate information
Appreciate languages and cultures of other peoples, dispelling prejudice and promoting biblical hospitality
Knowledge of people, events, and movements in history (including church history) and other cultures
A creative, versatile, analytic mind that pursues lifelong learning
Solve complex problems by thinking critically and creatively
Understand opposing worldviews and possess apologetic skills to defend their faith
Competencies to pursue their college and career goals
disciples: A personal, saving relationship with Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior
A strong moral compass that glorifies God in mind, heart, and activity
Scholarly knowledge of the Bible and ability to study and apply Scripture to all of life
Commitment to growth in faith through study, prayer, and fellowship
A heart of service motivated by love for God and humankind
Ability to share their faith with others
Appreciation for the natural environment and responsible stewardship of creation
influencers: Readily and humbly influence others by faith, compassion, and service
Intelligence and skills to build positive, cooperative, effective relationships
Pursue their unique passions and gifts to influence culture for Christ through excellence
Actively engaged in the church and community, serving God and others
Display a consistent Christian world-and-life view in all they do

graduation_requirements.note: Two tracks: standard graduation and College Prep. College entrance requirements often exceed these.

departments.note: Must include one life-science lab and one physical-science lab (chemistry/physics)
Must include World History, US History, and Government/Economics
Jr/Sr varsity athletes may substitute by semester
Required for standard track starting with freshmen entering 2028-29 (2.0 years)

special_programs.FFA: All Agricultural Education students are automatically enrolled in FFA; Ag courses require FFA activities and Supervised Agricultural Experience (SAE) projects.
special_programs.dual_credit_program: Students may earn high school and college credit concurrently. Offered through Waubonsee Community College and Lewis University. Some dual-credit classes are taught at Yorkville Christian High School by qualified YCHS teachers; WCC Plano courses are taken at the Plano campus. Students must be at least 16 to earn college credit unless an underage waiver is completed. Credit transfers to all Illinois colleges/universities; grades appear on both the HS and college transcripts. Weighted with a 1.0 GPA escalator. Families are charged the costs associated with dual-credit courses (except YCHS-taught dual-credit tuition, which the school pays).

waubonsee_community_college.type: Dual enrollment / Engineering-CAD tracks (see the 'Engineering (Waubonsee CC - Plano)' department for course descriptions)

honors_criteria.general: Honors courses target students with well-developed reading/writing skills, emphasizing critical thinking, synthesis, and presentation. No in-class remediation is assumed. Placement is reassessed yearly and is faculty-recommended with weighted grades (0.5 GPA escalator).
language_arts: Top national 25th percentile in Language Usage AND Reading on MAP or PreACT (or equivalent)
Independence, focus, work ethic; consistent completion
Positive, teachable attitude; strong analytical/evaluative skills in written and spoken word
Presents ideas logically and persuasively; identifies/summarizes key points; responds critically
Strongly organized writing following standard English conventions
math_geometry_algebra2: Strong problem-solving skills; makes connections; draws conclusions from data
A- or higher in the previous math course
Top national 25th percentile in Math on MAP or PreACT (or equivalent)
ap_calculus_additional: 80%+ on latest Precalculus Final OR 90%+ on Precalculus assessments
science_biology_chemistry: Strong problem-solving; makes connections; draws conclusions from data
A- or higher in the previous science course
Top national 25th percentile in Science on MAP or PreACT (or equivalent)
Honors Chemistry also requires A- or higher in Algebra I and Geometry
us_history: A- average in World History coursework
Independence, focus, work ethic; consistent completion
Positive, teachable attitude; strong analytical/evaluative skills
Presents ideas logically/persuasively; critical response to text; standard English conventions
spanish_2: Independence, focus, work ethic; positive, teachable attitude; appreciation for Spanish culture and desire to expand proficiency

departments.name: Agriculture
departments.note: All students auto-enrolled in FFA; FFA + SAE required. Intro to Agriculture is the prerequisite for all other Ag courses.

courses.name: Introduction to Agriculture
courses.description: Learn how the agriculture industry is organized; its major components; the economic influence of agriculture at state, national, and international levels; and the scope/types of agricultural careers. Covers basics of animal science, plant science, soil science, horticulture, natural resources, agribusiness management, and agricultural mechanics. (FFA activities and SAE projects are an integral component.)

courses.name: Animal Science I
courses.description: Develops understanding of the livestock (beef, dairy, sheep, goats, swine), poultry, and equine industries. Topics: scientific investigations, genetics, animal anatomy and physiology, nutrition, reproduction, animal health, and meat science.

courses.name: Agricultural Business 1
courses.subtitle: Business/Management
courses.prerequisite: Introduction to Agriculture OR Animal Science OR Horticultural Science
courses.description: Understanding of the agricultural industry relative to the US and world marketplace. Units: business ownership types, planning/organizing the agribusiness, financing, records, operations, agricultural law, taxes, and employability skills. Emphasis on math, reading comprehension, writing, and computer/workplace skills. (FFA activities and SAE projects are an integral component.)

courses.name: Agricultural Business 2
courses.subtitle: Entrepreneur/Communication
courses.prerequisite: Introduction to Agriculture OR Animal Science OR Horticultural Science
courses.description: Knowledge/skills in Agricultural Sales, Agribusiness Marketing, and Commodity Marketing. Units: economic principles, marketing/advertising, product development, sales techniques, communicating with employees/customers, managing risk, international agribusiness, and studying agricultural companies and careers. (FFA activities and SAE projects are an integral component.)

courses.name: Environmental Science
courses.description: Explores the natural-resources industry: interrelationships between natural resources, environmental systems, and humans; scientific principles of natural resources; environmental and natural-resource management; outdoor skills, safety, and ethics; outdoor recreation; energy; and waste management. (FFA activities and SAE projects are required.)

courses.name: Introduction to Ag Mechanics
courses.description: Introduces different agricultural-mechanics areas: safety, electricity, small engines, construction, plumbing, and surveying. (FFA activities and SAE projects are required.)

courses.name: Introduction to Food Science
courses.description: Applies scientific knowledge and processes to food development and preservation. Units: principles of food preservation, food processing, biochemistry of foods, food selection, and consumer health. Careers examined: meat inspector, quality-control technician, food processor, sanitation supervisor. (FFA activities and SAE projects are an integral component.)

courses.name: Horticultural Science & Landscaping
courses.description: Introduces the horticulture industry and basic plant science: horticulture research/careers, plant anatomy, seed germination, plant propagation, growing media, pest management, hydroponics, plant identification, greenhouse crops, and floral design. Landscaping: identifying landscape plants, designing plans, growing from seed, and maintaining landscaping and rain gardens. Agribusiness units on pricing, managing a horticulture business, advertising, and sales. (FFA activities and SAE projects are an integral component.)

departments.name: Biblical Studies
departments.note: Four sequential year courses (Bible I-IV) plus a 0.5-credit Bible elective (Book of Acts or Book of Romans).

courses.name: Bible I: Dynamic Christian Living
courses.description: Explores the basic elements of Christianity: salvation, biblical truths, prayer, and living out one's faith. A solid foundation for students new to the faith and those maturing toward a personal relationship with Christ.

courses.name: Bible II: Study of Matthew
courses.description: Studies the life of Jesus through the Gospel of Matthew. Students gain a theological foundation for following Christ, learn to study the Bible with depth, memorize key verses, and study the Lord's Prayer and the Apostles' Creed.

courses.name: Bible III: Behold Your God
courses.description: A study of God's character and attributes: that God is holy, righteous, and worthy of praise, and desires to know us. Students discover the blessing of relationship with Him.

courses.name: Bible IV: LEAD / Culture & Theology
courses.description: Semester 1: God's eternal plan and purpose for the earth and the student's role in His mission; unpacking unique talents and stewarding them into strengths. Semester 2: identifying the tension between God's eternal plan and a disintegrated culture, and applying one's unique calling in this generation.

courses.name: The Book of Acts
courses.description: Inductive Bible study of Acts: meaning and application, communicating the gospel and one's testimony, memorizing key verses. Discussion- and community-based, with Christian student-leadership experience.

courses.name: The Book of Romans
courses.description: Inductive Bible study of Romans: meaning and application, communicating the gospel and one's testimony, memorizing key verses. Discussion- and community-based, with Christian student-leadership experience.

courses.name: Adobe Photoshop / Illustrator
courses.description: Basics of Illustrator and Photoshop applied to a variety of projects: program interface, tools, illustration, image manipulation, file types.

courses.name: Introduction to Business
courses.description: Foundational business concepts and philosophies in free/open and stringent markets: management strategies, marketing (incl. digital), accounting/finance basics (balance sheets, inventory, depreciation), securities markets and regulation, economics, ethics and social responsibility, human resources, advertising/promotion (brick-and-mortar vs e-commerce), distribution, international business, and entrepreneurship with SWOT analysis.

courses.name: 3D Rendering and Design
courses.description: Introduction to 3D rendering in Blender: program basics, design concepts, and printing work on 3D printers for review.

courses.name: Speech
courses.description: College dual-credit course in human, interpersonal, and group communication. Students deliver introductory, informative, persuasive, and narrative content, culminating in a job/scholarship interview, and work in teams to deliver a cohesive message.

courses.name: Mass Communications
courses.description: College dual-credit course analyzing the nature and impact of media on society: theories, uses/impacts, research, ethics, and social responsibility. Historical developments in print, radio, film, television, internet technologies, public relations, and advertising, plus business practices and legal controls.

courses.name: Critical Film Analysis
courses.description: Introduces film as an art form through four production elements: cinematography, art direction, sound production, and editing, plus narrative style. Students view scenes and full-length films to critically analyze and dissect the production elements. (Listed as Semester 2 in the department index; described as Sem 1.)

courses.name: Yearbook / Journalism
courses.description: Hands-on creation of the school yearbook from concept to publication: photography, graphic design, layout, digital publishing, journalism principles, storytelling, and marketing. No prior experience required.

courses.name: Drawing
courses.description: Basic understanding of 2D art; students keep an active sketchbook, showcase presentations for peers, and collaborate using peer feedback for growth.

courses.name: Painting
courses.description: Color theory and applied painting skills; students showcase presentations for peers and collaborate using peer feedback for growth.

courses.name: Theater Showcase
courses.description: Stage performance through exercises and drills for stage acting, moving, and singing; each student prepares a performance for a live showcase as part of their final grade.

courses.name: Freshman Literature and Composition
courses.description: Survey/application of functional grammar progressing to advanced concepts (sentence structure, diction, punctuation, capitalization). Introduces literary works by American, British, and European writers. Composition progresses from sentence to paragraph to short creative writing. Frequent reading/writing with spelling and vocabulary emphasis; introductory ACT/SAT English skills.

courses.name: Honors Freshman Literature and Composition
courses.description: For strong, independent learners. Nurtures understanding and appreciation of literature from a Christian worldview around themes of journey and coming of age. Develops vocabulary and critical writing across genres; collaboration and technology for presentation skills.

courses.name: Sophomore Literature and Composition
courses.description: Studies genres of increasing complexity; reads/responds to fiction and non-fiction; integrates language and grammar with oral and written work. College/career readiness in reading, writing, listening, speaking, with global perspectives; intermediate ACT/SAT English skills.

courses.name: Honors Sophomore Literature and Composition
courses.description: Deep literary analysis and advanced writing for independent learners. Focuses on influential American and British authors; critical reading, writing, and public-speaking projects with technology. Central focus: comparing/contrasting authors' themes with biblical truth; vocabulary development.

courses.name: Junior Literature and Composition
courses.description: Continues critical reading and strong writing. ACT/SAT preparation across Usage/Mechanics (punctuation, grammar, sentence structure) and Rhetorical Skills (strategy, organization, style); sharpens writing for the essay portion of the ACT/SAT.

courses.name: Honors Junior Literature and Composition
courses.description: Builds on honors sophomore skills. Focuses on several influential American authors; critical reading and responding to literature through writing and speaking. Discovers themes/messages, examines connections, and compares/contrasts with biblical truth. Expects engaged, self-motivated readers of complex material.

courses.name: Senior Literature and Composition
courses.description: Focuses primarily on British Literature across historical periods. Explores key authors and literary movements as a basis for students' own writing and speaking; examines styles, techniques, and themes; engages in literary criticism of short stories, novels, and poetry. Authors may include O'Brien, Shakespeare, Shelley, Orwell, and Whitman.

courses.name: Honors Senior Literature and Composition
courses.description: Challenging preparation for college-level literary study and the AP test. Reads varied texts exposing students to styles, authors, and techniques; examines the writer's use of language and its effect on the reader; considers structure and themes; develops students' own writing across styles.

courses.name: Newsprint / Journalism
courses.description: Foundational training in gathering, reporting, and writing news for print and digital media: compelling leads, interviews, and ethical standards in developing campus news.

departments.name: Mathematics
departments.requirement: 3.0 credits required (must include Algebra and Geometry)

courses.name: Algebra I
courses.description: Develops algebraic skills and concepts for advanced courses, with problem-solving emphasis. Topics: operations with real numbers, linear equations and inequalities, relations and functions, polynomials, algebraic fractions, nonlinear equations.

courses.name: Geometry
courses.description: Properties and applications of common geometric figures in 2D and 3D; transformations and right-triangle trigonometry; writing proofs; inductive and deductive reasoning with real-world applications.

courses.name: Honors Geometry
courses.description: In-depth geometry that solidifies and extends concepts, introduces new ones, and applies algebra in geometric settings. Introduces proofs; topics include lines/angles, triangles, quadrilaterals, circles, area, and volume. Differs from regular geometry in depth of discussion and discovery.

courses.name: Algebra II
courses.description: Builds on algebraic and geometric concepts. Advanced algebra: systems of equations, advanced polynomials, imaginary/complex numbers, quadratics, and trigonometric functions; introduces matrices and their properties.

courses.name: Honors Algebra II
courses.description: Comprehensive honors course preparing for pre-calculus and calculus. Topics: conic sections; functions/relations and their graphs; quadratic, inverse, advanced polynomial, rational, radical, exponential, and logarithmic functions; sequences and series.

courses.name: Trigonometry
courses.description: Trig identities, graphing transformations of trig functions, and using laws of trig to solve for angles and sides of triangles; continued graphing-calculator exploration.

courses.name: Pre-Calculus
courses.description: Builds on Algebra 2 with a focus on trigonometry; introduces combinatorics, probability, and induction proofs. In-depth techniques and applications with technology to prepare for advanced coursework.

courses.name: AP Calculus AB
courses.prerequisite: Grade of B or higher in Pre-Calculus
courses.fees: $100 for the required AP exam in May
courses.description: Yearlong college-level course preparing for the AP Calculus AB exam: precalculus review; limits, derivatives, definite integrals, and differential-equation modeling, and their applications. Multi-representative approach (numerical, graphical, verbal, analytical) with technology.

courses.name: Health and Wellness
courses.description: Semester-long course on how the body functions and the importance of wise decisions to protect health and well-being. Beyond physical health, covers mental/emotional, social, and spiritual health: stress management, communication and relationships, body image, coping skills, safety, and dealing with peer pressure and difficult situations.

courses.name: Sports Performance
courses.description: High-intensity class for students serious about improving skills for high school and college athletics: hand-eye coordination, jumping ability, speed, agility, and strength. Students track progress, attendance, body-fat percentage, food intake, and sprint times. Students with other activities that limit full participation should not enroll; grading is partly based on attendance and quarterly progress, with weekly communication between the Sports Performance teacher and coaching staff.

courses.name: Intro to Team Sports
courses.description: Rules, skills, fundamentals, and strategies across a variety of individual and dual sport activities. Health, safety, and sportsmanship are emphasized and assessed.

courses.name: Competitive Team Sports
courses.description: Participation in a variety of competitive team sports at an advanced level of activity, performance, and skill development.

courses.name: Life Skills 101
courses.description: Introduces several basic life skills including (but not limited to): goal setting; personal finance and budgeting; consumer awareness; investing and retirement; insurance (health, life, home, auto); auto maintenance and simple repairs; resumes, interviewing, and workplace etiquette; and domestic skills (utilities, rental agreements). Builds confidence to navigate the world independently.

courses.name: Teacher Assistant
courses.description: Students may serve as a Teacher's Assistant (TA) for faculty or staff during a regularly scheduled class period. Requires a form approved first by the faculty/staff member and then by the parent. Earns 0.5 elective credit, open to juniors and seniors, limited to one per semester.

departments.name: Science
departments.requirement: 3.0 credits required (one life-science lab + one physical-science lab)

courses.name: Biology
courses.description: Introduction to living organisms, how they function, and how they interact in the biosphere: ecology, biochemistry, cells (structure, division, energy usage), human body systems, genetics, bacteria and viruses, and an introduction to plants.

courses.name: Honors Biology
courses.description: Inquiry-centered laboratory biology stressing life processes in greater depth. Students are guided through the scientific process and examine all levels of biological organization from molecules and cells to populations and ecosystems.

courses.name: Chemistry
courses.description: Basic general chemistry: atomic structure, chemical symbols/formulas/equations, equation calculations, phases of matter, algebraic manipulations, molecular structure, and solution chemistry; lab safety, basic lab skills, and computer-assisted labs.

courses.name: Honors Chemistry
courses.note: Honors placement also requires A- or higher in Algebra I and Geometry
courses.description: In-depth exploration via labs, note-taking, and discussion. Topics: chemistry equipment/techniques, elements and compounds, gases, thermodynamics, structure of matter, periodic table, math used in chemistry, the metric system, chemical bonds and intermolecular forces, balanced equations, stoichiometry, and the scientific method.

courses.name: AP or Dual Credit Chemistry
courses.note: Department index lists it as 'AP or Dual Credit Chemistry'; the detail page lists 'Dual Credit Chemistry' (grade 11-12, 1.0 credit) with no course description.

courses.name: Physics
courses.description: In-depth, collaborative, project-based physics: mechanics in one and two dimensions, momentum and energy, waves and light, electricity and magnetism, subatomic physics, and cross-curricular earth-science topics.

courses.name: Anatomy and Physiology
courses.description: Full-year lab course in human anatomy and physiology from a Christ-centered perspective. Uses microscope investigations, lab exercises, and extensive dissections. Topics: histology, organ systems, homeostasis, health, development, injury/pathology, disease diagnosis/treatment, medical imaging, and drug action, with a culminating cadaver-lab trip. Prepares students for medicine, nursing, research, EMT, physical therapy, pharmacy, and sports training.

departments.name: Social Sciences
departments.requirement: 3.0 credits required (must include World History, US History, and Government/Economics)

courses.name: Geography
courses.description: Reviews US states/capitals and studies other continents, countries, and capitals; mapping skills. Focuses on climates, landforms, culture, history, and environment of regions; resources produced by other countries and their impact on the US; religions of each country compared/contrasted with Christianity.

courses.name: World History
courses.description: Major themes of world history beginning with the Renaissance and Enlightenment in Europe, using maps and geographic tools. Connects the past with the present and future.

courses.name: U.S. History
courses.note: Students must pass a Constitution Test
courses.description: Chronological US history from early European colonization and government formation to present day. Activities include text reading, map analysis, debate, inquiry, research, presentation, media, and current-event discussion.

courses.name: Honors U.S. History
courses.prerequisite: Selection by social studies department and administration
courses.description: Covers US history from the precolonial period to the present, with emphasis on 20th-century economic/diplomatic interactions, the Great Depression, and the World Wars. Develops analytical skills (cause and effect, media impact, multiple perspectives); relies on Christian faith and morality to evaluate events; enhances communication through writing and presentations. Built to state standards.

courses.name: U.S. Government
courses.description: Workings of American government and the Constitution and citizens' responsibilities toward God, one another, and country. Focuses on the federal government with exposure to state and local government; challenges Christians to be involved in government.

courses.name: Economics
courses.description: Basic understanding of the US economic system, classical and Keynesian economics, and responsibilities toward God and fellow man. Introduces other current world theories; hands-on investing and factors influencing the stock market.

courses.name: Psychology and Sociology
courses.description: Humanities-level introduction covering psychology, sociology, and social work; a chance to fulfill a college-level humanities requirement in a Christian setting. Sociology is the study of people in groups: the structure, function, and behavior of human society, with emphasis on the interaction between society and its members and how the individual is affected by society. Topics include social institutions, gender issues, marriage and the family, adolescence, the adult world, mass media, and deviance, discrimination, and inequality. Students design and conduct a social research project.

courses.name: Street Law
courses.description: Introduction to the law and legal systems of the United States. Major focal points: constitutional law, general legal principles, civil and criminal law, the courts, court procedures, and civil rights; additional topics may include family law, housing law, and consumer law. Real-world experiences deepen understanding of government, individual rights, and legal disputes, using case studies, mock trials, contemporary issues, current events, and legal research applied to students' everyday lives.

departments.name: World Language
departments.requirement: Elective (2.0 years required for College Prep; required for standard track starting 2028-29)

courses.name: Spanish I
courses.description: First-year introduction to Spanish language and culture. Emphasis on listening, speaking, reading, and writing; communicating on daily-life topics via paired practice, small groups, and role plays; geography and culture of Spanish-speaking countries; expressing feelings/opinions, describing people/things/places, making requests, and asking/answering simple questions.

courses.name: Spanish II
courses.description: Builds on Spanish 1 vocabulary, grammar, and culture; improves listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Communicates on topics of life, travel, sports, food, and culture.

courses.name: Honors Spanish II
courses.prerequisite: Grade of A or higher in Spanish I and a placement test
courses.description: Deeper study toward independent use of the language and critical thinking in listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Strengthens grammar and vocabulary with depth and complexity at an accelerated pace; continues geography, history, food, and culture of Spanish-speaking countries.

departments.name: Engineering (Waubonsee CC - Plano)
departments.note: Waubonsee Community College dual-credit Engineering/CAD track taught at the WCC Plano campus. All courses are dual credit (1.0 GPA escalator); students must be 16+ to earn college credit. See special_programs.dual_credit_program.

courses.name: Introduction to Engineering
courses.description: Introduction to the engineering profession, including the wide variety of fields of study and potential careers. Covers general engineering theory and an overview of different engineering fields; students learn to use computer-aided design software and lab equipment within the engineering design process.

courses.name: Engineering Graphics
courses.description: Introduction to engineering and design: drafting, dimensioning, tolerancing, fasteners, and descriptive geometry. Topics include multi-view orthographic representations, principal auxiliary views, section views, and production drawings for part models. At least 50% of the course requires Computer-Aided Drafting and Design (CAD).

courses.name: AutoCAD I
courses.description: Introduces computer-aided drafting using AutoCAD to set up drawings and add lines, circles, arcs, other shapes, geometric constructions, and text. Students use display and editing techniques to obtain information about their drawings, work with drawing files, and examine basic dimensioning concepts.
